lessons.title: The sovereignty of God in creation

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: Orders at a food stall
steps.narration: Imagine an akara seller setting up her stall. She decides what goes where. In Genesis, we see who gives the orders when the world begins.

steps.title: God brings order by speaking
steps.display: God commands light and separates it from darkness.
steps.narration: Why start with who gives the order? That tells you what sovereignty means here. Think of the person in charge of opening a school gate. In Genesis, God has authority over what he makes.

steps.title: Sky, land and plants
steps.display: On day two God separates the waters with the firmament. On day three dry land appears and the earth brings forth plants.
steps.narration: The order helps you answer questions about what came first. Picture clearing a patch before planting beans. Here you see ground before anything grows on it. The space dividing the waters belongs to the day before.

steps.title: Lights mark time
steps.display: On day four God makes the lights to mark seasons, days and years.
steps.narration: Watch the job these lights do. You might use a calendar to work out when school closes. Here the lights help mark time. If a question says light first appeared on day four, go back to day one.

steps.title: Life on days five and six
steps.display: Fish and birds appear on day five. Land animals and humans appear on day six.
steps.narration: A simple grouping keeps the days straight. Picture sorting fish and chickens from goats at a market. In this account water creatures and birds share a day. Land animals and people come the next day. Check that grouping before you choose.

steps.title: The seventh day is set apart
steps.display: God blesses and sets apart the seventh day because he rests from his work on it.
steps.narration: The reason helps you place the seventh day. Picture marking a day differently on your calendar because a long task is finished. In Genesis, look for what has already ended before the day is set apart.

steps.title: Human responsibility
steps.display: God makes humans in his image and gives them dominion over living creatures. The man in Eden is to tend and keep the garden.
steps.narration: Pay attention to the job that goes with human authority. If someone puts you in charge of a school garden, you have real work. The tasks in Eden help you see what responsibility looks like.

steps.title: God’s authority over nations
steps.display: Jeremiah compares God’s authority over Israel to a potter’s power over clay and applies the lesson to nations.
steps.narration: Why visit a potter? The clay gives you a picture you can see. Imagine a potter reshaping a bowl that slumps. Now watch the passage turn from the workshop to what God says about the choices nations make.

steps.title: The Creator’s authority reaches the earth
steps.display: In Isaiah, the Lord says he made the earth, created humans and stretched out the heavens. He declares that there is no God beside him.
steps.narration: Why does Isaiah mention what God has made? It helps explain the reach of his authority. Picture looking at a map that includes more than your own street. Follow how the passage moves from the earth to the heavens.

steps.title: Worked question
steps.display: Which event belongs to day three?
working: A. God separates light from darkness
B. God separates the waters with the firmament
D. God makes the lights to mark seasons
steps.narration: Before you work through the choices, find the day number the stem asks for. Put the surrounding days in order on your scrap paper. The answer will be the event between those clues.

steps.title: Follow the creation sequence
steps.display: Answer C · Dry land appears
working: A. That happens on day one. (Genesis 1:3-5)
B. That happens on day two. (Genesis 1:6-8)
C. Day three is when the gathered waters leave dry land visible. (Genesis 1:9-13)
D. That happens on day four. (Genesis 1:14-19)
steps.narration: Use the day numbers to cut down your choices. Light comes first, so cross that off. The space between the waters comes next. The lights that mark time come later. We need the point when ground comes into view.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: JAMB-style practice · What work does God give the man in Eden?
working: B. To name the light Day
C. To gather the waters into seas
D. To separate the waters with the firmament
steps.narration: First look for a task one person can do. That gives you a way to set aside the choices about the whole world. Then find the verse that gives the reason for placing him there.

steps.title: Identify the garden task
steps.display: Answer A · To keep the garden
working: A. God places him there to tend it and keep it. (Genesis 2:15)
B. God gives the light that name. (Genesis 1:5)
C. God gathers the waters and names the seas. (Genesis 1:9-10)
D. God makes the firmament to divide the waters. (Genesis 1:6-8)
steps.narration: The question asks about a human job. That clue removes the choices about forming the world. Put your finger on the reason the man is placed in the garden. The verse gives you his work right there.

steps.title: Light and the lights
steps.display: Light appears on day one. The lights that mark time are made on day four.
steps.narration: Those two details sound alike in a hurry. Before you pick an answer, circle the job named in the question. Is it about day and night beginning, or about what marks the passing of time?

steps.title: The Creator gives the orders
steps.display: God directs the order of creation.
steps.narration: When a question gives you many details, find the one who acts first. The commands help you see who is in charge. Then match the result of each command to its place in the account.

quickCheck.stem: Practice · What does God do on the seventh day?

options.why: That belongs to day six. (Genesis 1:24-31)

options.text: Makes the lights to govern day and night
options.why: That belongs to day four. (Genesis 1:14-19)
That belongs to day two. (Genesis 1:6-8)
God ends his work and rests on the seventh day. (Genesis 2:1-3)

lessons.title: The covenants with Noah, Abraham and Israel, and the new covenant

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: A promise you can remember
steps.narration: Picture a tailor giving you a slip after you order a uniform. It helps you remember the promise. Watch for signs and promises in this lesson.

steps.title: Noah and the flood
steps.display: God tells Noah to build an ark after seeing the earth’s violence. The flood comes and those with Noah in the ark survive.
steps.narration: The warning explains why the building mattered. Picture putting your books somewhere high when rain starts entering a room. Here the danger had been announced in advance. Follow the passage from the warning to the people who survived.

steps.title: The bow and Noah’s covenant
steps.display: God makes a covenant, a binding promise or agreement, with Noah, his descendants and living creatures. The bow marks the promise against another flood destroying all flesh.
steps.narration: A binding promise or agreement is called a covenant. Start with who is covered. Think of a notice meant for every family in a compound. Here the promise reaches beyond Noah’s household to living creatures too.

steps.title: Abraham and his descendants
steps.display: God promises Abraham descendants and land, gives circumcision as the covenant sign, and says the covenant will continue with Isaac.
steps.narration: The family line matters because the promise looks ahead. Circumcision here means removing the foreskin. Think of how a school crest identifies a group. Keep the sign of the agreement distinct from the child named to carry it forward.

steps.title: The promise to Abraham reaches beyond his household
steps.display: God calls Abram to leave his country and promises that all families of the earth will be blessed in him.
steps.narration: Why look past Abram’s own household? Imagine one family receiving help and then seeing the benefit reach an entire compound. Read the call alongside the promise. The journey begins with one person, but notice how far the blessing reaches.

steps.title: Israel at Sinai
steps.display: Israel agrees to obey God. Moses reads the book of the covenant and sprinkles the people with covenant blood.
steps.narration: Listen to both sides here. At a class meeting, a teacher might read rules and ask pupils to follow them. Find what the people agree to in Exodus. Then notice what happens as Moses confirms the agreement.

steps.title: Sinai ties agreement to conduct
steps.display: God gives Israel commands including keeping the sabbath and forbidding theft.
steps.narration: A promise to obey only makes sense if you know what has been asked. Think of a game where the rules are read before play. In Exodus, read the commands as the content of the commitment the people take on.

steps.title: Jeremiah contrasts the new covenant with the old
steps.display: Jeremiah says the new covenant will differ from the covenant that the people broke after God brought them out of Egypt.
steps.narration: The contrast matters because it tells you why Jeremiah calls this promise new. Think of comparing two agreements a class made at different times. Read what happened to the earlier one first. Then check what God promises to do differently.

steps.title: The new covenant and the heart
steps.display: Jeremiah links the new covenant to God’s law written in people’s hearts and forgiveness of sin.
steps.narration: Imagine knowing your school pledge by heart. You can remember it without looking at the wall. That helps you picture the inward change Jeremiah describes. The promise also addresses the wrongs people have already done.

steps.title: A new heart and spirit
steps.display: Ezekiel describes God cleansing the people and giving them a new heart and spirit so they follow his ways.
steps.narration: A change inside matters because it changes what you do. Suppose you start returning borrowed pencils even when nobody checks. In Ezekiel, God does the changing. Watch how the promise moves from cleansing to a different way of living.

steps.title: Worked question
steps.display: Which sign does God give for the covenant with Noah?
working: B. The bow in the cloud
C. Blood sprinkled on the people
D. God’s law written in the heart
steps.narration: An agreement can have a promise and a visible reminder. Look for the reminder here. Then ask which person is named in the question. You can use that name to rule out other agreements.

steps.title: Match the covenant with its sign
steps.display: Answer B · The bow in the cloud
working: A. God gives this sign in the covenant with Abraham. (Genesis 17:9-11)
B. God says the bow marks his covenant involving the earth. (Genesis 9:12-17)
C. Moses does this in the covenant ceremony with Israel. (Exodus 24:6-8)
D. Jeremiah gives this as a feature of the new covenant. (Jeremiah 31:31-33)
steps.narration: Begin with whose promise you are matching. The mark on the body goes with Abraham. The blood belongs with Moses and the people. Jeremiah points you inward. That leaves the sign you could see overhead.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: JAMB-style practice · Which promise does Jeremiah attach to the new covenant?
working: A. No flood will again destroy all flesh
B. Canaan will be given to Abraham and his descendants
C. The people will be sprinkled with covenant blood
D. God will forgive their iniquity
steps.narration: Start by finding the promise connected to a change within the people. The other choices may come from familiar scenes. Find the one that fits the prophet’s message about what God will do.

steps.title: Distinguish the new covenant
steps.display: Answer D · God will forgive their iniquity
working: A. This promise belongs to the covenant with Noah. (Genesis 9:11)
B. This is part of God’s promise to Abraham. (Genesis 17:7-8)
C. This describes what Moses does when Israel agrees to obey. (Exodus 24:3-8)
D. Jeremiah includes forgiveness in the new covenant. (Jeremiah 31:31-34)
steps.narration: Start by naming the speaker whose message you need. Then test each choice against that message. Some choices belong to real agreements you have studied. Your job is to find the one Jeremiah actually gives.

steps.title: A sign and a promise do different jobs
steps.display: The bow is the sign. The promise concerns a flood destroying all flesh.
steps.narration: Notice what a question wants you to name. If you are asked for the sign, look for what a person could see. If you are asked for the promise, look for what God says about the future.

steps.title: Match the promise to the people
steps.display: Each passage identifies the people and the terms of its covenant.
steps.narration: Give yourself one sorting question before you look at the options. Who is the agreement with? Get that clear first. Then you can check what was promised and whether the passage gives a sign.

quickCheck.stem: Practice · With which son does God say he will establish his covenant with Abraham’s family?

options.why: God names Isaac as the son with whom he will establish it. (Genesis 17:19-21)
God promises to bless Ishmael but names Isaac for the covenant. (Genesis 17:18-21)
Jacob is a son of Isaac in the set passage. (Genesis 25:19-26)
Esau is Isaac’s other son, born before Jacob. (Genesis 25:19-26)

lessons.title: Leadership qualities of Joseph, Moses, Joshua and the judges

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: Leading when things get hard
steps.narration: Think of your class prefect when assembly gets noisy. Does she plan, speak up or ask for help? Watch what each leader does.

steps.title: Joseph plans for famine
steps.display: Joseph credits God for Pharaoh’s answer and proposes storing grain in the years of plenty. Pharaoh puts him in charge.
steps.narration: Planning matters most while you still have choices. Imagine setting aside some rice before you run short. Joseph sees a good season as a chance to get ready. Notice who he credits before offering advice.

steps.title: Joseph reassures his brothers
steps.display: Joseph tells his brothers God sent him ahead to preserve life.
steps.narration: Listen for what Joseph wants his brothers to understand. If a teammate who wronged you comes for help, you can choose how to respond. Joseph uses his position to reassure his family and explain how lives were saved.

steps.title: Moses speaks for the people
steps.display: God sends Moses to bring Israel out of Egypt. After the spies’ report, Moses appeals to God to pardon the people.
steps.narration: A leader may need to speak on behalf of others. Imagine a prefect asking the head teacher to spare classmates a penalty. Here Moses brings the people’s case before God. Notice the reasons he gives when he asks for mercy.

steps.title: Joshua keeps the law in view
steps.display: God tells Joshua to be courageous and to obey the law given through Moses.
steps.narration: Courage needs a direction. Think of a new class captain who checks the school rules before settling a quarrel. Joshua has a new job too. Notice that the charge to be brave comes with instructions about what to follow.

steps.title: Joshua follows the instructions at Jericho
steps.display: Joshua passes on the instructions about marching round Jericho. On the seventh day the people shout and the wall falls.
steps.narration: Instructions matter in this story because timing changes the action. Picture a team waiting for its captain’s signal before starting. Notice when the people must stay quiet. Then look for Joshua’s signal and what happens when the people shout.

steps.title: Joshua asks about defeat at Ai
steps.display: After Israel’s defeat at Ai, Joshua appeals to God. God identifies Israel’s breach of the command about the devoted things.
steps.narration: A setback gives you a different view of a leader. Picture a captain asking what went wrong after losing a match. Here Joshua asks God, and the reply turns his attention to the people’s conduct. Follow that change in focus.

steps.title: Joshua asks Israel to choose whom to serve
steps.display: At Shechem, Joshua calls on Israel to serve the Lord and declares that his own household will do so.
steps.narration: A leader’s words can show what they commit themselves to. Think of a captain agreeing to the same team rule everyone else must follow. Here Joshua calls for a choice and then announces where his own family stands.

steps.title: Deborah gives direction
steps.display: Deborah judges Israel and summons Barak to lead the force against Sisera. She agrees to go with Barak.
steps.narration: Listen for who gives the direction and who gathers the force. A team captain can name the plan while another player leads a move. Deborah’s agreement to go also helps you see what her support looked like.

steps.title: Gideon acts despite fear
steps.display: Gideon pulls down his father’s altar of Baal at night because he fears his household and the men of the city.
steps.narration: Watch what Gideon does with his fear. Imagine asking a teacher privately about a problem you feel nervous raising. The time you choose can tell us how you feel. Gideon still carries out the task assigned to him.

steps.title: Gideon’s call to deliver Israel
steps.display: The Lord sends Gideon to save Israel from Midian and promises to be with him despite Gideon’s doubts about his standing.
steps.narration: The person chosen may doubt that he is ready. Imagine a pupil who thinks the class captain would never pick him. Notice what Gideon says about his family and himself. Then read the assurance that answers his objection.

steps.title: Samson’s role is announced before his birth
steps.display: The angel tells Samson’s mother that her son will begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines.
steps.narration: The word begin helps you understand the size of the task. Imagine a pupil starting a job the whole class will have to finish. Look at the problem Israel faces when the messenger arrives. Then listen for the role the child is given.

steps.title: Samson asks for strength
steps.display: After Delilah learns his secret and Samson is captured, he asks God for strength before pulling down the house.
steps.narration: The ending matters because Samson knows he needs help. Picture someone asking for a hand before lifting a heavy bench. In this account, listen for whom Samson asks. Read that prayer before you answer what leads into his last act.

steps.title: Worked question
steps.display: Who proposed storing grain before the famine?
steps.narration: A future shortage is the problem the leader must solve here. Look for the person who hears about it while there is still plenty. Then choose the action that makes sense with that timing.

steps.title: Find the leader who planned ahead
steps.display: Answer A · Joseph
working: A. He proposes collecting and storing food during the good years. (Genesis 41:33-36)
B. He pleads for pardon after the people rebel over the spies’ report. (Numbers 14:1-4, 11-19)
C. She summons Barak and gives the direction for the campaign against Sisera. (Judges 4:4-7)
D. He pulls down his father’s altar of Baal. (Judges 6:25-28)
steps.narration: Use the problem in the question to sort the leaders. Moses pleads after a rebellion. Deborah gives a battle command. Gideon takes down an altar. Look for the one who could see a food shortage coming.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: JAMB-style practice · What does Moses ask God to do after Israel reacts to the spies’ report?
working: A. Appoint Joshua before the congregation
C. Show a sign with a fleece
D. Give him strength once more
steps.narration: Time is your best clue. Find the scene with the spies and the people’s reaction. Then ask what the leader sought for others at that point. Leave the details about later scenes aside.

steps.title: Recognize a leader’s request
steps.display: Answer B · Pardon the people’s iniquity
working: A. That happens in a later scene about Moses’ successor. (Numbers 27:15-23)
B. Moses appeals to God’s mercy and asks him to pardon them. (Numbers 14:17-19)
C. Gideon asks for those signs. (Judges 6:36-40)
D. Samson makes that request before bringing down the house. (Judges 16:28-30)
steps.narration: Put yourself at the moment after the report. What problem does Moses need to address right then? A successor and a fleece belong to other scenes. Here the people have rebelled, and Moses speaks up for them.

steps.title: Deborah and Barak
steps.display: Deborah summons Barak and later signals the time to act. Barak gathers the men and pursues Sisera’s host.
steps.narration: Two people can share a victory and do different jobs. If an option swaps their actions, it can still sound familiar. Check whose words set things in motion and whose movements you follow in the battle.

steps.title: Compare what each leader does
steps.display: Leadership is shown through actions such as planning, pleading for others and giving direction.
steps.narration: Give each leader a verb before you try to memorise a list of qualities. Ask what the person actually did. That gives you a detail you can point to when two options both sound admirable.

quickCheck.stem: Practice · Whom does Moses set before Eleazar and the congregation as his successor?

options.why: Aaron is given to Moses as a spokesman in a different scene. (Exodus 4:14-16)
Deborah summons Barak for the campaign against Sisera. (Judges 4:4-7)
Moses lays hands on Joshua and gives him a charge before the congregation. (Numbers 27:18-23)
Pharaoh places Joseph over Egypt. (Genesis 41:39-43)

lessons.title: Obedience and disobedience, and their results

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: Following the instruction
steps.narration: Your auntie asks you to buy two cups of garri. Do you follow her instruction? Watch what people do after they hear a command.

steps.title: Abraham and Isaac
steps.display: Abraham obeys the test, God stops him from harming Isaac, and Abraham offers a ram. God renews the promise of blessing.
steps.narration: Why does the order of events matter? It shows where the test ends. Picture a referee stopping a drill before contact. Keep your eye on what Abraham is stopped from doing. Then check which offering actually goes ahead.

steps.title: The three youths and the furnace
steps.display: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refuse to worship the king’s image. They are thrown into the furnace and come out unharmed.
steps.narration: Their choice matters because they make it before knowing the outcome. Think of refusing to join classmates who are cheating. Here the three men face the king’s threat together. Listen for what they say even if rescue does not come.

steps.title: David seeks direction at Ziklag
steps.display: David asks God whether to pursue the raiders. God tells him to pursue, and David recovers what was taken.
steps.narration: Watch how David handles pressure before he moves. Imagine checking with your coach before chasing a ball into the road. The question comes first in David’s story. Then you can follow the action and see how it ends.

steps.title: Adam and the command
steps.display: God forbids eating from one tree. Adam eats, and God sends him out of Eden.
steps.narration: Start with the instruction, so you can see what decision broke it. Think of a clearly marked rule for one cupboard at home. Find the boundary God gives the man, then follow what happens after he crosses it.

steps.title: Manna on the seventh day
steps.display: The people gather twice as much on day six. Moses tells them to set some aside. Some go out on day seven and find none.
steps.narration: Timing is the clue here. Think of buying food the day before a market closes. The extra supply has a purpose. If a question asks why people found nothing, check the day they chose to go out.

steps.title: Israel and the golden calf
steps.display: The people ask Aaron for gods while Moses is away. They worship the calf and face punishment.
steps.narration: Notice what the people say about Moses before they make their request. Think of a group changing a plan when its leader is late. Their impatience helps you follow the story. Then look at what they choose to worship.

steps.title: Moses at the rock
steps.display: God tells Moses to speak to the rock. Moses strikes it twice. God says Moses and Aaron will not bring the assembly into the land.
steps.narration: A result can happen even when someone ignores part of an instruction. Imagine getting an answer right after using a method your teacher ruled out. The people still get water. Check what God told Moses to do before it came.

steps.title: Saul and Amalek
steps.display: Saul spares Agag and the best animals despite the command. Samuel says God has rejected him as king.
steps.narration: The excuse matters here because Saul says the animals were for an offering. Think of finishing only part of an errand and explaining why. Check the original instruction before you accept the explanation. Samuel measures Saul against that command.

steps.title: Worked question
steps.display: Which action disobeys the instruction at the rock?
steps.narration: To know whether an act breaks a rule, you need to know the rule first. Read what God asks for at the rock. Check each choice against that before you consider what the crowd received.

steps.title: Compare the command and the action
steps.display: Answer D · Striking the rock twice
working: A. God specifically tells Moses and Aaron to speak to it. (Numbers 20:7-8)
B. God tells Moses to gather the people. (Numbers 20:8)
C. God directs Moses to take the rod. (Numbers 20:8-9)
D. Moses strikes it although the command says to speak to it. (Numbers 20:8, 11-12)
steps.narration: Read the command before looking at the result. Speaking was required. Gathering the people was required too. Taking the rod was also part of the order. Check what Moses actually did with it when the people were watching.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: JAMB-style practice · What reason does Samuel give for Saul’s rejection as king?
working: A. He went out to gather manna on the seventh day
B. He rejected the word of the Lord
C. He made a golden calf
D. He struck the rock twice
steps.narration: Look for Samuel’s explanation because the question asks for a reason. Start with the words spoken after Saul returns. If an option sounds familiar from a different account, ask where you heard it.

steps.title: Match disobedience to its consequence
steps.display: Answer B · He rejected the word of the Lord
working: A. Some Israelites did this and found none. (Exodus 16:27-30)
B. Samuel links the loss of the kingdom to Saul’s disobedience. (1 Samuel 15:19-23)
C. Aaron makes the calf after the people’s request. (Exodus 32:1-4)
D. Moses does this in the wilderness. (Numbers 20:7-12)
steps.narration: Start with the person named in the stem. That clears away several real events which belong to other accounts. Now listen to Samuel’s judgment. He makes a direct link between Saul’s choice and what Saul loses.

steps.title: Taking the rod and using it
steps.display: Taking the rod is commanded. Striking the rock replaces the commanded act of speaking to it.
steps.narration: A question can put two details from the same scene side by side. Find the instruction about each action. The fact that Moses had the rod does not tell you how he was meant to use it.

steps.title: Connect action to outcome
steps.display: Read the instruction, then compare the response and its result.
steps.narration: Make three small boxes on your scrap paper. Put what was asked in the first and what happened in the next. Use the last box for the outcome. That keeps a familiar name from leading you to the wrong story.

quickCheck.stem: Practice · What happened when some Israelites went out to gather manna on the seventh day?

options.why: The passage says the people who went out found nothing. (Exodus 16:27)

options.text: They gathered twice the usual amount
options.why: The double amount was gathered on the sixth day. (Exodus 16:22)

options.text: They first received instructions to bake and boil
options.why: Moses gave those instructions before the day of rest. (Exodus 16:23)

options.text: They were told to look for manna in the field that day
options.why: Moses says there would be none in the field that day. (Exodus 16:25-26)

lessons.title: Social justice, true religion and divine love in Amos and Hosea

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: Fair prices and fair scales
steps.narration: Imagine a yam seller who sings beautifully but cheats with her scales. Which action shows how she treats people? Keep that question in mind.

steps.title: Amos exposes dishonest trade
steps.display: Amos describes traders who want to make the measure small, raise the price and cheat with false balances.
steps.narration: The details show you how the poor were harmed. Picture paying full price for a measure of garri that is too small. Check both what the traders take and what they give. Their scales are part of the wrong.

steps.title: Amos calls for justice at the gate
steps.display: Amos condemns taking bribes and turning aside the poor at the gate. He calls for justice there.
steps.narration: Why pay attention to the gate? It is where the passage places decisions that can wrong poor people. Imagine an official hearing a complaint and taking money to favour one side. Check what Amos asks the people to replace that with.

steps.title: Amos connects worship and justice
steps.display: God rejects Israel’s feasts, offerings and songs in Amos and calls for justice and righteousness.
steps.narration: Why does Amos talk about songs beside fair treatment? Imagine singing at an assembly after cheating a classmate. A good performance cannot fix what you did. Watch for the change in conduct that the passage calls for.

steps.title: Amos warns of exile
steps.display: Amos tells people who live at ease and ignore Joseph’s suffering that they will go into captivity.
steps.narration: Comfort can make it easy to miss someone else’s trouble. Think of eating your lunch while a classmate beside you goes hungry. Amos addresses people who enjoy plenty and feel no grief. Look for the consequence he announces.

steps.title: James describes true religion in action
steps.display: James names caring for orphans and widows in trouble and keeping oneself unstained by the world as marks of pure religion.
steps.narration: How can a lesson about worship reach the street you live on? Think of helping a neighbour who has nobody to fetch water. James gives you people to notice. He also asks you to pay attention to your own conduct.

steps.title: Hosea shows love after unfaithfulness
steps.display: God tells Hosea to love a woman described as an adulteress, comparing this to God’s love for Israel despite its turning to other gods.
steps.narration: The comparison helps you see what makes the love striking. Imagine someone making room for a teammate who walked away. In Hosea, Israel has turned elsewhere. Notice who keeps loving and who is expected to come back.

steps.title: Hosea calls Israel to return
steps.display: Hosea calls for Israel to return, ask forgiveness and give up reliance on Assyria and idols. God promises to heal their waywardness and love them freely.
steps.narration: Returning involves more than saying sorry. Think of admitting you copied homework and choosing to do the next task yourself. Listen for what Israel says it will stop trusting. Then look at what God offers to do.

steps.title: Hosea names what is lacking
steps.display: Hosea says there is no truth, mercy or knowledge of God in the land. God desires mercy and knowledge of him above sacrifice.
steps.narration: Why put mercy beside offerings? A pupil might bring a gift to school and still bully someone. The gift alone tells you little about the pupil’s conduct. In Hosea, notice what God says he wants from the people.

steps.title: Worked question
steps.display: Which trading practice does Amos condemn?
working: D. Seeking good so that the people may live
steps.narration: Put yourself beside the buyer. Ask which choice would leave you paying more than the goods were worth. Then check the list of practices Amos describes. A single detail about measurement can settle this one.

steps.title: Identify the practice Amos condemns
steps.display: Answer A · Making the measure smaller
working: A. Amos says the traders want to shrink the measure and cheat with false balances. (Amos 8:4-6)
B. Hosea says God desires mercy. (Hosea 6:6)
C. James names care for widows among the marks of pure religion. (James 1:27)
D. Amos urges the people to seek good. (Amos 5:14-15)
steps.narration: Look first for something a seller can do at the stall. Showing mercy is praised in Hosea. Helping widows is praised in James. Seeking good is encouraged in Amos. That leaves the choice that gives the buyer less.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: JAMB-style practice · What does Israel say about Assyria in Hosea’s appeal to return?
working: C. Assyria will not save Israel
D. Assyria will forgive Israel’s wrongs
steps.narration: Listen for the change in allegiance as the people return. They speak about what they will give up. See if you can find the words about a nation before you pick an answer.

steps.title: Follow Hosea’s call to return
steps.display: Answer C · Assyria will not save Israel
working: A. Israel is to say that Assyria will not save it. (Hosea 14:1-3)
B. God promises to heal Israel’s waywardness. (Hosea 14:4)
C. Israel gives up reliance on Assyria when it returns to God. KJV calls it Asshur here. (Hosea 14:1-3)
D. Hosea directs the people to ask God to take away their iniquity. (Hosea 14:1-2)
steps.narration: Look at what Israel is asked to say on returning. The passage sends us to God for healing and pardon. That helps you tell whose help is being sought and whose help is being given up.

steps.title: Keep the prophet and image together
steps.display: Amos pictures justice flowing like water. Hosea’s marriage scene pictures God’s love for Israel despite its unfaithfulness.
steps.narration: Attach a picture to each speaker. A flowing stream takes you to the call for fair dealing. The marriage takes you to the passage about love through betrayal. That will help when both prophets appear in the choices.

steps.title: Test worship against conduct
steps.display: The passages link devotion to God with justice and mercy in daily life.
steps.narration: When an option sounds religious, ask what it means for the people nearby. Do they get a fair deal? Does someone in trouble get help? These passages give you ways to recognise what their speakers value.

quickCheck.stem: Practice · Which action does James include in pure religion?

options.why: Amos condemns the traders who want to do this. (Amos 8:4-6)

options.text: Visiting orphans and widows in their trouble
options.why: James names this as part of pure religion. (James 1:27)
Hosea calls on Israel to give up that reliance. (Hosea 14:1-3)

options.text: Hearing the word without acting on it
options.why: James tells his readers to do what the word says. (James 1:22-25)

lessons.title: Holiness and divine call of the prophets

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: Being sent with a message
steps.narration: Imagine your head teacher sends you to deliver a message. Who sent you? What must you say? Ask both questions about each prophet.

steps.title: Isaiah sees God’s holiness
steps.display: Isaiah sees the Lord on a throne. The seraphim proclaim the Lord holy, and Isaiah recognises his own unclean lips.
steps.narration: Being holy here means being set apart and wholly pure. Think of noticing ink on your hand against clean white paper. That picture helps you see why Isaiah notices his own fault. Listen for what he says about his lips.

steps.title: Isaiah is cleansed and sent
steps.display: A seraph touches Isaiah’s lips with a live coal and says his sin is purged. Isaiah offers to go and receives a message for the people.
steps.narration: The order helps you understand why the coal matters. Picture someone cleaning a cut before you go back to play. In Isaiah’s vision, the burning piece touches the very place he has mentioned. Afterward, listen for his reply to God.

steps.title: Ezekiel eats the scroll
steps.display: Ezekiel eats the written scroll, which tastes sweet as honey, and is sent to speak God’s words to Israel.
steps.narration: You need to take in a message before passing it on. Imagine learning a school announcement before carrying it to another class. Ezekiel gets a vivid picture of taking it in. Notice the taste even though the writing describes sorrow.

steps.title: Ezekiel must speak despite resistance
steps.display: God sends Ezekiel to a rebellious people. Ezekiel is to speak God’s words whether they listen or refuse.
steps.narration: The listeners’ reaction could easily discourage a messenger. Picture reading a notice to a noisy class. Your job is still to make the announcement. That helps you hear the distinction between Ezekiel’s task and the people’s response.

steps.title: Jeremiah receives words and an assignment
steps.display: Jeremiah says he is a child. God touches his mouth, gives him words and appoints him over nations and kingdoms.
steps.narration: Why does Jeremiah mention his age? He thinks he cannot speak. Imagine a younger pupil worried about delivering a school message. Look at what God gives Jeremiah for the task. His ability is answered before his assignment is described.

steps.title: Worked question
steps.display: In whose call does a live coal touch the messenger’s lips?
working: D. The people who hear Ezekiel
steps.narration: The object in the question matters more than the fact that someone is speaking for God. Picture it by itself. Then recall which account puts it near the prophet before he is sent.

steps.title: Match the messenger and the object
steps.display: Answer B · Isaiah
working: A. He eats a scroll before speaking to Israel. (Ezekiel 3:1-4)
B. A seraph brings the coal from the altar and touches his lips. (Isaiah 6:6-7)
C. God touches Jeremiah’s mouth with his hand. (Jeremiah 1:9)
D. They are the people Ezekiel is sent to address after eating the scroll. (Ezekiel 3:1-4)
steps.narration: Focus on what is used. Ezekiel takes in writing, so remove him. Jeremiah feels a hand, so remove him too. Ezekiel’s listeners receive a message. Find the prophet who describes what the seraph brings from the altar.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: JAMB-style practice · What does God tell Ezekiel to do if the people refuse to listen?
working: A. Wait until they ask for the message
B. Speak his own words instead
C. Be silent because they are rebellious
D. Speak God’s words even then
steps.narration: Before deciding, ask who controls the response to a message. The people may choose to refuse what they hear. Now check what God expects the messenger to do when that happens.

sources.where: Ezekiel 2:7; Ezekiel 2:7; Ezekiel 3:4; Ezekiel 2:3-7; Ezekiel 2:7; Ezekiel 3:10-11

steps.title: Find the duty when people resist
steps.display: Answer D · Speak God’s words even then
working: A. The command applies whether they hear or refuse. (Ezekiel 2:7)
B. God tells Ezekiel to speak God’s words. (Ezekiel 2:7; Ezekiel 3:4)
C. God identifies the rebellion and still sends him. (Ezekiel 2:3-7)
D. Ezekiel must give the message regardless of their response. (Ezekiel 2:7; Ezekiel 3:10-11)
steps.narration: Ask which part of the task Ezekiel can actually do. He can deliver what he was given. The crowd decides whether to hear it. Scan the options for the one that leaves the assignment in place.

sources.where: Ezekiel 2:7; Ezekiel 2:7; Ezekiel 3:4; Ezekiel 2:3-7; Ezekiel 2:7; Ezekiel 3:10-11

steps.title: Two mouths, two actions
steps.display: A seraph touches Isaiah’s lips with a coal. God touches Jeremiah’s mouth with his hand.
steps.narration: Both scenes direct your attention to speech. That similarity can pull you toward a wrong option. Ask who reached out and what touched the prophet. Then check what the act means in that particular scene.

steps.title: Follow the call to the assignment
steps.display: Each account connects what God gives the prophet with the message he is sent to deliver.
steps.narration: For each prophet, ask two questions as you read. What prepares this person to speak? What is the person sent to say or do? The second question keeps you from remembering only the striking object.

quickCheck.stem: Practice · Which prophet says he cannot speak because he is a child?

options.why: Isaiah says his lips are unclean. (Isaiah 6:5)
Ezekiel is told to eat the scroll and speak to Israel. (Ezekiel 3:1-4)
Jeremiah gives his youth as his reason for saying he cannot speak. (Jeremiah 1:6-7)
A seraph brings a coal in Isaiah’s vision. Jeremiah is the one who objects that he is a child. (Isaiah 6:6-7; Jeremiah 1:6)

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: Sort by what happened
steps.narration: Imagine sorting plantain and yam at a market stall. You put each kind together. We can sort these stories by what Jesus does.

steps.title: Nature miracle at sea
steps.display: Jesus rebukes the wind and speaks to the sea from the boat. A great calm follows.
steps.narration: Why did the disciples ask who he was? Picture the sudden quiet after a storm has rattled your roof. Their question follows a change they could see and hear. In an exam, the boat helps you locate the scene.

steps.title: Nature miracle and the crowd
steps.display: About five thousand men sit down to eat. The food available at the start is five barley loaves and two small fish, and twelve baskets of pieces remain.
steps.narration: The numbers help you track the change, so keep them in separate groups. Picture counting the food before a school picnic and collecting leftovers afterward. In John, check what is brought first and what the disciples gather at the end.

steps.title: Jesus walks on the sea
steps.display: The disciples see Jesus walking on the sea as they travel by boat. He tells them who he is and says they should not fear.
steps.narration: The location of each person tells you which story you are in. Picture waving from the bank while a friend sits in a canoe. Now read John carefully. Where are the disciples, and where is Jesus when they first see him?

steps.title: Water becomes wine at Cana
steps.display: At a wedding in Cana, Jesus has servants fill waterpots with water. The ruler of the feast tastes wine.
steps.narration: Notice the servants because they know something the feast leader does not. Imagine carrying a drink from the kitchen to a party table. You know what went into the jug. Follow who filled the pots and who tasted what came out.

steps.title: Lazarus at Bethany
steps.display: Lazarus has been in the grave four days when Jesus arrives. Jesus calls him out of the grave.
steps.narration: The time detail identifies this account. Imagine marking four days on a wall calendar. John includes that count before the call at the grave. Look for the way Lazarus comes out too. That gives you another clue to recognise the passage.

steps.title: Jesus raises Jairus’ daughter
steps.display: Jesus goes into Jairus’ house and takes the girl by the hand. She rises, and he tells them to give her food.
steps.narration: Coming back to life in these stories is called resuscitation. Think of a scene you can picture inside a single room. In Luke, follow Jesus from the message on the road to his instruction after the girl gets up.

steps.title: Jesus raises the widow’s son
steps.display: At the gate of Nain, Jesus has compassion on a widow and raises her only son.
steps.narration: This time the setting helps you recognise the story. Imagine people meeting at the gate of a compound. Here one group is leaving town when Jesus approaches. Notice whose grief Jesus sees before he speaks to the young man.

steps.title: Healing and thanks
steps.display: Jesus tells ten people with leprosy to show themselves to the priests. All are cleansed as they go, and one returns to give thanks.
steps.narration: Watch the numbers at two points. Think of ten pupils sent on an errand and one coming back to thank you. The smaller number answers who returned. It does not give you the number whose skin condition was healed.

steps.title: The man at Bethesda
steps.display: Jesus tells the man at Bethesda to pick up his bed and walk. The man does so.
steps.narration: The bed lets you picture the change. Imagine a mat that someone was lying on and can now carry away. In John, read the man’s reply about getting to the water first. Then notice exactly what Jesus asks him to do.

steps.title: The centurion trusts Jesus’ word
steps.display: The centurion says Jesus only needs to speak and his servant will be healed. Jesus commends his faith and the servant is healed.
steps.narration: Ask why the officer thinks a word is enough. Think of a teacher sending an instruction to another classroom. The officer uses his own experience of giving orders to explain his confidence. Listen for how Jesus responds to that confidence.

steps.title: A man born blind washes at Siloam
steps.display: Jesus sends a man born blind to wash at Siloam. The man washes and returns able to see.
steps.narration: A named place can guide you as quickly as a bus stop on a familiar route. In this account the man is sent somewhere. Look for what Jesus puts on his eyes before you check where he goes to wash.

steps.title: Bartimaeus receives sight near Jericho
steps.display: In Mark, Bartimaeus calls out as Jesus leaves Jericho, and Jesus restores his sight.
steps.narration: Notice the name and the direction of travel. Picture checking whether your bus is coming into town or leaving it. That small clue is worth keeping when you compare Mark with another account. Also listen for Bartimaeus’ request.

steps.title: Jesus frees the man with unclean spirits
steps.display: Jesus permits the unclean spirits called Legion to enter swine.
steps.narration: Driving out an evil spirit is called exorcism. A small detail can locate the right story, like a landmark on your way to school. Look for the pigs here and check who asks for permission before they enter them.

steps.title: Jesus commands a spirit to leave a boy
steps.display: A father brings his son to Jesus after the disciples cannot drive out the spirit. Jesus commands it to leave.
steps.narration: Why does the father turn to Jesus? Imagine asking for help again after the first person you ask cannot fix a problem. In Mark, check what the father says about the disciples. Then look at what Jesus tells the spirit.

steps.title: Worked question
steps.display: Who is raised at Nain?
steps.narration: Place names help you sort stories with a similar outcome. Find the name given here, then picture the people Jesus meets there. Which person’s story has both the setting and the action you need?

steps.title: Use the place clue
steps.display: Answer C · The widow’s only son
working: A. John places this event at Bethany. (John 11:1, 17-18, 43-44)
B. Luke places the raising in the house Jesus enters. (Luke 8:41-42, 49-56)
C. Jesus meets his funeral procession at the gate of Nain. (Luke 7:11-15)
D. This servant is healed in the centurion account. (Matthew 8:5-13)
steps.narration: Start with the town, then test each scene. Lazarus points you to Bethany. Jairus takes you into a house. The servant belongs to a healing. Look for the account where a crowd meets Jesus on its way out.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: JAMB-style practice · According to Mark, what does Jesus do when the disciples wake him during the storm?
working: A. He rebukes the wind and speaks to the sea
B. He walks towards the boat on the sea
C. He tells the servants to fill waterpots
D. He tells the man to take up his bed
steps.narration: Picture where Jesus is at the start. If the others have to wake him, they can reach him already. Use that small clue to separate this story from the other account involving a boat.

steps.title: Separate the miracles at sea
steps.display: Answer A · He rebukes the wind and speaks to the sea
working: A. The wind ceases and calm follows. (Mark 4:38-39)
B. That is another event in Mark, after the feeding. (Mark 6:41-50)
C. This happens at the wedding in Cana. (John 2:1-7)
D. That is the healing at Bethesda. (John 5:2-9)
steps.narration: You can narrow it down from the opening action. They wake Jesus, so he is with them already. That clears away the scene where he approaches the boat. Now look for what changes the weather in this account.

steps.title: Near Jericho or leaving it
steps.display: Mark places Bartimaeus’ healing as Jesus leaves Jericho. Luke places his account of a blind man’s healing as Jesus comes near Jericho.
steps.narration: Direction words are easy to skim past. Picture reading a bus sign and checking whether you are heading into town or out. Do the same with the verse. Use the Gospel named in the question to choose the direction.

steps.title: Match action, person and place
steps.display: A named person and setting help distinguish miracles of the same kind.
steps.narration: When two options involve someone coming back to life, the result alone cannot settle it. Look for the clue that belongs only to that passage. It might be the person’s relation to someone else or where the event takes place.

quickCheck.stem: Practice · At which miracle do servants fill waterpots?

options.why: Jesus feeds the crowd, and his disciples gather the leftovers there. (John 6:9-13)
Jesus tells the man to take up his bed and walk. (John 5:2-9)

options.text: Healing of the man born blind
options.why: Jesus sends the man to wash in Siloam. (John 9:6-7)
Jesus directs the servants to fill the pots at Cana. (John 2:1-9)

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: A story with a point
steps.narration: Imagine a teacher tells a story about sharing groundnuts to explain fairness. Listen to Jesus’ stories for the point each one helps you see.

steps.title: Parables and the hearer
steps.display: Jesus explains to his disciples why he teaches in parables and contrasts those who perceive with those who hear without understanding.
steps.narration: A short story told to make a point is called a parable. Think of a tale you heard that only made sense after a second listen. Here, pay attention to the people hearing the story. Jesus draws a distinction between their responses.

steps.title: The sower and the soils
steps.display: The seed represents the word. In Matthew, good ground represents the hearer who understands and bears fruit.
steps.narration: Start with what happens to the seed, because each result points to a response. Think of planting beans in hard ground and loose soil. The growth differs. In Matthew’s explanation, look for what understanding leads the hearer to produce.

steps.title: The weeds and the harvest
steps.display: Jesus explains that the harvest in the story of the weeds represents the end of the world.
steps.narration: The timing answers a question the servants raise. Picture waiting until harvest before sorting what came up in a field. At first the two plants grow together. Read Jesus’ own explanation to see what the moment of separation represents.

steps.title: The drag-net and the catch
steps.display: People sort good fish from bad after drawing in the net. Jesus compares this to separation at the end.
steps.narration: The full catch helps you see why sorting comes later. Picture fishers bringing their net to shore before separating the fish. Now look at what Jesus says the angels will do. That connects the fishing scene with his point.

steps.title: The wedding garment
steps.display: A king invites guests to his son’s wedding. A guest without a wedding garment is thrown out.
steps.narration: Arrival and readiness are different details. Picture reaching a school sports day without the kit you need. Look at the guest who is already inside. The king’s question tells you which detail about that guest matters in the story.

steps.title: The lost sheep, coin and son
steps.display: Luke links finding the sheep and coin to joy over a sinner who repents. The father celebrates the return of his lost son.
steps.narration: Turning away from wrongdoing is what repenting means. Picture the relief when you find a missing purse after searching. Luke puts that feeling beside a person returning. Look for repeated moments of celebration, including what the father says to the older son.

steps.title: The neighbour who acts
steps.display: In the Good Samaritan, a Samaritan cares for the injured man after a priest and a Levite pass by. Jesus asks who acted as neighbour.
steps.narration: Focus on what someone does when there is a need. Picture stopping to help a pupil who fell when others kept walking. At the end Jesus changes the focus of the question. Look at who showed mercy through action.

steps.title: The rich man and Lazarus
steps.display: In the parable, poor Lazarus lies at a rich man’s gate. After their deaths the rich man suffers and Lazarus is comforted.
steps.narration: Put both parts of the story side by side. Picture the same two people at the beginning and at the end of a play. Here their situations change sharply. Check what Abraham says about the warnings the brothers already have.

steps.title: The rich fool and bigger barns
steps.display: A rich man plans larger barns for his crops. God says his life is required that night, and Jesus warns about storing wealth for oneself.
steps.narration: The plan sounds good until you ask what the man leaves out. Picture counting savings for years you assume you will have. His time is cut short in the story. Look at the question God asks about the things he has prepared.

steps.title: The widow who keeps asking
steps.display: The widow’s repeated plea is answered. Jesus uses the judge’s response to ask whether God will give justice to people who cry to him day and night.
steps.narration: Why does she keep going back? Think of a pupil who follows up on a request that was ignored. The repeated visits give you the point. Notice how the judge finally answers and what Jesus asks us about God.

steps.title: The Pharisee and the publican
steps.display: Jesus contrasts the Pharisee’s self-praise with the tax collector’s plea for mercy. The tax collector goes home justified, or counted right with God.
steps.narration: A publican was a tax collector. Picture two pupils explaining themselves to a teacher. One brags and the other asks for help. Listen for the difference in the prayers. It prepares you for Jesus’ judgment at the end.

steps.title: Worked question
steps.display: Who acts as neighbour to the injured man?
steps.narration: Go back to the road and watch what each traveller does. Try answering before you read the last verse. Then see whether Jesus’ closing question directs you to the same person you picked.

steps.title: Identify the neighbour by his action
steps.display: Answer B · The Samaritan
working: A. He sees the man and passes by on the other side. (Luke 10:31)
B. He treats the wounds and arranges care at an inn. (Luke 10:33-37)
C. He looks and then passes by. (Luke 10:32)
D. The Samaritan asks the innkeeper to care for the man. The traveller who shows mercy first is the Samaritan. (Luke 10:33-37)
steps.narration: Check for the person who stops and takes responsibility. The priest keeps going. The Levite leaves too. The innkeeper enters after the man has been brought in. Now look at who notices the need and begins to help.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: JAMB-style practice · Which parable teaches people to keep praying and avoid giving up?
working: A. The Pharisee and the publican
D. The widow and the unjust judge
steps.narration: Before you choose, think about the kind of action that shows someone will keep asking. Repetition is your clue here. Two choices deal with prayer, but only one puts that repeated action at the centre.

steps.title: Tell the two prayer stories apart
steps.display: Answer D · The widow and the unjust judge
working: A. Jesus uses this story to contrast self-praise with asking for mercy. (Luke 18:9-14)
B. Jesus uses this story to warn about living for possessions. (Luke 12:15-21)
C. The story concerns a king’s invitation and a guest who lacks the required garment. (Matthew 22:1-14)
D. The widow keeps asking, and Jesus speaks of people crying to God day and night. (Luke 18:2-8)
steps.narration: Look at what makes the judge finally respond. That helps you sort the options. Two stories here involve prayer. The one you want uses a woman’s repeated visits to make its point about keeping on.

steps.title: Two stories with rich men
steps.display: The rich fool plans bigger barns. In the story of Lazarus at the gate, the rich man asks Abraham to send a warning to his brothers.
steps.narration: A wealthy character is a clue you still need to sharpen. Look for what the person asks or plans. Building more storage belongs to one story. A plea about family members after death takes you to the other.

steps.title: Connect the story to its lesson
steps.display: Use Jesus’ explanation or the stated purpose to connect a parable’s details to its main point.
steps.narration: Ask what the story helps the hearer see. Then check whether the passage gives you an explanation. That is better evidence than a detail you simply find memorable. Use it to settle the point before you choose.

quickCheck.stem: Practice · In Jesus’ explanation of the sower in Matthew, who is the good ground?

options.text: The hearer who understands and bears fruit
options.why: Jesus uses good ground for this response to the word. (Matthew 13:23)

options.text: The hearer who fails to understand and loses what was sown
options.why: Jesus connects this response to the wayside. (Matthew 13:19)

options.text: The hearer who falls away under persecution
options.why: This describes the stony places. (Matthew 13:20-21)

options.text: The hearer whose response is choked by cares and riches
options.why: Jesus connects this response to the thorns. (Matthew 13:22)

lessons.title: The trials, death and resurrection of Jesus

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: Put the accounts in order
steps.narration: Think of putting pictures from your school’s cultural day in order. Each shows a different scene. We’ll follow who appears and what happens next.

steps.title: The hearing before the high priest
steps.display: Before Caiaphas and the council, Jesus is questioned about being the Christ, the Son of God. The high priest accuses him of blasphemy.
steps.narration: Words said about God can become a serious charge in this hearing. The charge is called blasphemy here. Imagine a school panel asking someone to say plainly who they claim to be. Look at how the high priest reacts to the reply.

steps.title: The hearing before Herod
steps.display: Pilate sends Jesus to Herod. Herod wants to see a miracle, gets no answer and sends Jesus back after he and his soldiers mock Jesus.
steps.narration: Track who sends Jesus where. Imagine tracing the way a paper goes from one office to another and back. The return helps you remember Herod’s role. Look at what Herod hoped to see and how Jesus responds.

steps.title: Pilate and Barabbas
steps.display: Pilate says he finds no fault deserving death. The crowd asks for Barabbas, and Pilate hands Jesus over to be crucified.
steps.narration: Compare the judgment with the action that follows. Picture a referee saying there was no foul but still giving a penalty. In Luke, watch how the voices of the crowd matter. Also check which prisoner goes free.

steps.title: Crucifixion at Golgotha
steps.display: Jesus is crucified at Golgotha, with two others beside him. The title over him identifies him as King of the Jews.
steps.narration: Being put to death on a cross is called crucifixion. A sign can tell you what a scene is about, like a name board outside a shop. In John, read the title and notice who objects to how it is written.

steps.title: Jesus’ words at death
steps.display: John records Jesus saying “It is finished”. Luke records Jesus entrusting his spirit to the Father.
steps.narration: The Gospel named in a question matters when you are asked who records a saying. Think of filing two notes under different names. Read each scene up to Jesus’ death. Then match the line with the writer who gives it.

steps.title: Jesus addresses others from the cross
steps.display: Luke records Jesus asking the Father to forgive those involved and promising paradise to the man who appeals to him. John records Jesus entrusting his mother to the beloved disciple.
steps.narration: Ask who Jesus speaks to and who needs something in each scene. Then use the audience as your clue. Think of sorting letters by their addressee. Here you can distinguish a request to the Father from words to a man and to a disciple.

steps.title: Joseph’s role in the burial
steps.display: Joseph of Arimathaea asks Pilate for Jesus’ body and lays it in his own new tomb.
steps.narration: The move from cross to tomb introduces someone new. Picture a name on a doorway helping you remember who owns a room. In Matthew, take note of whose tomb it is and who gives permission for the burial.

steps.title: The women hear the news
steps.display: In Matthew, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary go to the tomb. An angel announces that Jesus has risen, and Jesus meets them on their way.
steps.narration: Coming back to life after death is called resurrection. Imagine hearing news first and then meeting the person it is about. Matthew moves through those two moments. Notice what the women are asked to do after hearing the news.

steps.title: Jesus appears to Thomas
steps.display: Thomas wants to see Jesus’ wounds. Jesus later speaks to him and calls those who believe without seeing blessed.
steps.narration: Evidence is what Thomas asks for. Picture arriving late and wanting to see what everyone else is talking about. Thomas says what would convince him. In the next scene, listen for what Jesus says about people who do not see.

steps.title: Jesus appears on the road to Emmaus
steps.display: Two disciples walk towards Emmaus with Jesus without recognising him. They recognise him when he breaks bread.
steps.narration: Recognition is the turning point. Picture a pupil hearing a familiar voice before seeing who is speaking. In Luke the two travellers spend time with Jesus before they know him. Check what he is doing when they recognise him.

steps.title: Jesus sends witnesses and ascends
steps.display: Jesus tells the disciples they will receive power and be witnesses. He is taken up and a cloud receives him out of their sight.
steps.narration: Going up is what ascension means here. Picture a teacher giving a group its task just before leaving. That order helps you connect two parts of Acts. Check what the disciples are told they will do after receiving power.

steps.title: Worked question
steps.display: Who sends Jesus back to Pilate after questioning him and wanting to see a miracle?
steps.narration: Names repeat across the hearings, so use the order of events. Follow Jesus away from Pilate and back again. Which person’s questions come between those movements? That gives you a place to start.

steps.title: Track the hearings
steps.display: Answer C · Herod
working: A. The high priest questions Jesus about his identity before the council. (Matthew 26:57-66)
B. He is the prisoner released at the crowd’s request. (Luke 23:18-25)
C. He hopes to see a miracle, then sends Jesus back to Pilate. (Luke 23:8-12)
D. He later asks Pilate for Jesus’ body. (Matthew 27:57-60)
steps.narration: The clue is what this person hoped to see. Caiaphas asks about Jesus’ identity. Barabbas is awaiting release. Joseph comes after the death. The hearing between Pilate’s appearances is the place to look for the man who wanted a sign.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: JAMB-style practice · What does Joseph of Arimathaea ask Pilate for in Matthew?
working: C. An answer to the charge of blasphemy
steps.narration: Before choosing, ask whether this request comes during a hearing or after Jesus has died. That will clear up several tempting choices. Then find the request Matthew records and see who receives it.

steps.title: Distinguish the burial from the hearings
steps.display: Answer A · The body of Jesus
working: A. Pilate orders that the body be given to Joseph. (Matthew 27:57-60)
B. The crowd asks for Barabbas at Jesus’ hearing. (Matthew 27:20-26)
C. The high priest raises that charge before the council. (Matthew 26:63-66)
D. Luke says Herod hopes to see Jesus perform a miracle. (Luke 23:8)
steps.narration: Pin the request to its place in the timeline. Joseph comes after the death. That takes you away from the hearing and the crowd’s choice. Look at what Joseph needs before he can use the tomb.

steps.title: Joseph and Barabbas have different roles
steps.display: Joseph of Arimathaea asks for Jesus’ body. Barabbas is the prisoner Pilate releases.
steps.narration: Both names appear near Pilate, so attach a different action to each. For one, think of the prisoner who walks free. For the other, think of the person who comes to arrange a burial.

steps.title: Put each witness and action in its scene
steps.display: Follow the sequence through hearings, death, burial, sightings of the risen Jesus and ascension.
steps.narration: Arrange the scenes before you try to remember the names. Then ask who speaks or acts in each one. That gives you a way to recover a detail even when the exam question starts in the middle.

quickCheck.stem: Practice · Who says he will not believe unless he sees the marks of the nails?

options.why: Pilate questions Jesus before the crucifixion. (John 18:33-38)
Thomas asks to see the wounds after the other disciples tell him they saw Jesus. (John 20:24-27)
Herod wants to see a miracle during his hearing. (Luke 23:8-9)
Mary tells the disciples she has seen the Lord after meeting him. (John 20:14-18)

lessons.title: Justification by faith, and the law and grace

steps.title: Picture it
steps.display: A gift and a wage
steps.narration: Picture earning money selling sachet water, then getting a gift from a friend. One is earned. Read Paul with that difference in mind.

steps.title: Justification is given through Christ
steps.display: Paul says all have sinned and people are justified freely by God’s grace through Christ. He distinguishes faith in Christ from works of the law.
steps.narration: Being counted right with God is called justification. A freely given favour is grace. Think of receiving a gift you could never earn as wages. In these verses, keep your eye on who gives it and where Paul places trust.

steps.title: Faith and confession
steps.display: Paul links believing that God raised Jesus from the dead and confessing Jesus as Lord with salvation.
steps.narration: To confess here means to say openly what you believe. Imagine saying aloud the answer you are convinced is right. Paul puts what a person believes beside what the person says. Check the passage for the content of both.

steps.title: Peace with God follows justification
steps.display: Paul says being justified by faith brings peace with God through Jesus Christ and gives believers hope.
steps.narration: A result matters because it tells you what has changed. Think of two people at peace after a quarrel is resolved. In this passage, Paul writes about the relationship with God. Follow the next verses to see how he speaks about hope.

steps.title: Christ’s death brings reconciliation
steps.display: Paul says God shows his love through Christ’s death for sinners and speaks of former enemies being reconciled to God.
steps.narration: Reconciliation means a broken relationship is restored. Think of two neighbours speaking again after a long quarrel. In Romans, look for what happens while people are still described as enemies. That timing shows how Paul is explaining God’s love.

steps.title: Abraham trusts God’s promise
steps.display: Abraham believes God can do what he promised. His faith is counted as righteousness, and Paul links the promise with faith rather than the law.
steps.narration: You can spot faith here by asking whose ability Abraham relies on. Imagine trusting a tailor who has promised to finish your uniform. Think about what makes you expect it to be ready. In Romans, Abraham counts on God to keep his promise.

steps.title: The law has a temporary role
steps.display: Paul says the law was added because of transgressions and calls it a schoolmaster leading to Christ. After faith comes, believers are no longer under that schoolmaster.
steps.narration: Transgressions are acts that break a command. Paul uses a guide to show how the law had a task. Think of someone who walks you to school while you are learning the route. Notice where the guide leads and when that role ends.

steps.title: Grace abounds where sin abounds
steps.display: Paul says the law enters so the offence might abound, and grace abounds even more. He contrasts the reign of sin in death with grace leading to life through Jesus Christ.
steps.narration: Keep your attention on which has the greater reach in Paul’s comparison. Picture a debt growing, then a gift large enough to cover it. Look at how the passage moves from the offence to the outcome it connects with Jesus.

steps.title: The blessing and the promise reach Gentiles
steps.display: Paul says Christ redeems from the curse of the law so the blessing of Abraham can reach Gentiles. Those who belong to Christ are heirs according to the promise.
steps.narration: Gentiles are people who are not Jews. An heir is someone entitled to receive what is passed down. Think of reading who is included in a family promise. Then see how Paul explains who shares in the blessing through Christ.

steps.title: Worked question
steps.display: According to Romans 5, what follows being justified by faith?
working: A. Peace with God through Jesus Christ
B. Being placed under a schoolmaster again
C. Being justified by works of the law
D. Receiving the promise through the law
steps.narration: Hold on to the difference between a cause and its result. Paul has already described how people are counted right. Now look for the change that follows. Check the opening line of the chapter named here.

steps.title: Identify a result of justification
steps.display: Answer A · Peace with God through Jesus Christ
working: A. Paul names peace with God as a result. (Romans 5:1)
B. Galatians says believers are no longer under that schoolmaster after faith comes. (Galatians 3:24-25)
C. Galatians says works of the law do not justify. (Galatians 2:16)
D. Paul links Abraham’s promise to the righteousness of faith. (Romans 4:13-16)
steps.narration: The question asks what follows, so watch for an outcome. The schoolmaster leads toward Christ. Keeping the law cannot supply the verdict here. Abraham’s promise is linked with trust. Now read the first verse for what changes in the relationship with God.

steps.title: JAMB-style practice question
steps.display: JAMB-style practice · What image does Paul use in Galatians for the law’s role in leading to Christ?
working: A. An heir who receives the promise
C. A curse from which there is no release
D. A free gift of justification
steps.narration: Look for a comparison about guiding someone for a time. That is the task Paul is describing. Several of these choices belong in his teaching, but only one does the job named in the stem.

steps.title: Identify Paul’s image for the law
steps.display: Answer B · A schoolmaster
working: A. Paul calls those who belong to Christ heirs. (Galatians 3:29)
B. Paul uses this image for the law’s role before faith comes. (Galatians 3:23-25)
C. Paul says Christ redeems people from the curse of the law. (Galatians 3:10-14)
D. Romans connects free justification with God’s grace through Christ. (Romans 3:24)
steps.narration: Ask what job the picture has to do. It has to lead somewhere. The heir receives something. The gift describes what is given. Look for the image that shows someone guiding a person toward a destination.

steps.title: Ground and result of justification
steps.display: Paul names grace through Christ and faith when discussing how people are justified. He names peace with God as a result.
steps.narration: Pause on the question word. If it asks how someone is counted right, look for the basis Paul gives. If it asks what follows, look for the change in the person’s relationship with God. The two questions lead to different verses.

steps.title: Paul ties justification to trust in Christ
steps.display: Paul teaches that God justifies freely through Christ and distinguishes faith from works of the law.
steps.narration: When you see Paul mention the law, ask what work it does in that passage. Then ask how someone is counted right with God. Keeping those questions clear helps you follow how the two ideas fit together.

quickCheck.stem: Practice · According to Romans 4, why was Abraham’s faith counted as righteousness?

options.text: He received the promise through the law
options.why: Paul says the promise came through the righteousness of faith. (Romans 4:13)

options.text: He believed God could perform what he had promised
options.why: Paul connects Abraham’s confidence in God’s promise to the counting of his faith as righteousness. (Romans 4:20-22)

options.text: He relied on his own body remaining strong
options.why: Paul mentions Abraham’s age and describes his confidence in God’s power to fulfil the promise. (Romans 4:19-22)

options.text: He gave up on the promise when his body was old
options.why: Paul says Abraham did not waver through unbelief. (Romans 4:19-21)
